new.title: Stand under the giant dinosaur at the Museum für Naturkunde
new.desc: The atrium is ruled by Giraffatitan, at more than 13 metres the tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton in the world, with the T. rex Tristan nearby. The museum also keeps the Berlin Archaeopteryx, the most complete specimen of the first bird, found in 1871.
new.tip: Do not miss the glass wing of the wet collection: about a million animals in alcohol, stored in 276,000 jars. Weekday mornings are calmest; school groups arrive around ten.

new.title: Meet the Romantics in the Alte Nationalgalerie
new.desc: Friedrich August Stüler designed this museum like a Roman temple raised on a high plinth, and it opened in 1876. Inside hang Caspar David Friedrich's The Monk by the Sea and Adolph Menzel's Iron Rolling Mill, plus French Impressionists.
new.tip: Head straight to the top floor for the Friedrich room before the crowds do. The colonnaded courtyard in front is a quiet place to sit even without a ticket.

new.title: See Schinkel's brick church full of marble statues
new.desc: Karl Friedrich Schinkel built the Friedrichswerdersche Kirche between 1824 and 1831 as an early Gothic Revival church in red brick. After years of closure caused by damage from nearby construction it reopened as a gallery of 19th century sculpture by Schadow, Rauch and Schinkel's circle.
new.tip: The upper gallery tells Schinkel's own story. Allow about an hour, and combine it with a walk along the Spree canal behind it.

new.title: Find the medieval Dance of Death in the Marienkirche
new.desc: Berlin's oldest parish church still in use stands alone under the TV tower, first recorded in the 13th century. In its tower hall runs a 22 metre Totentanz fresco, painted around the plague year of 1484, whitewashed during the Reformation and rediscovered in 1861. The alabaster pulpit is by Andreas Schlüter, 1703.
new.tip: The fresco is faint, so let your eyes adjust and follow Death dancing with pope, emperor and peasant alike. Entry is usually free outside services.

new.title: Walk through the 1957 showcase of the Hansaviertel
new.desc: For the Interbau exhibition of 1957, West Berlin invited star architects to rebuild this bombed quarter at the edge of the Tiergarten. Alvar Aalto, Walter Gropius, Oscar Niemeyer and Egon Eiermann each designed housing blocks set loosely among lawns and trees.
new.tip: Start at the Akademie der Künste on Hanseatenweg and wander with no plan; signs by the buildings name each architect. Niemeyer's block on stilts is on Altonaer Straße.

new.title: Admire the swooping roof of the 'pregnant oyster'
new.desc: The Haus der Kulturen der Welt was built in 1957 as the Kongresshalle, a gift from the United States designed by Hugh Stubbins. Its roof collapsed in 1980 and was rebuilt in the original form. Berliners nicknamed it the pregnant oyster, and Henry Moore's Butterfly sculpture stands in the pool outside.
new.tip: The terrace by the Spree is open to all and has a café. The exhibitions, concerts and festivals inside are often excellent, so check the programme.
new.q: Haus der Kulturen der Welt, John-Foster-Dulles-Allee 10, Berlin

new.title: Learn about the July plot at the Bendlerblock
new.desc: In the courtyard of this army headquarters, Claus von Stauffenberg and fellow officers were shot on the night of 20 July 1944 after their attempt on Hitler failed. The Gedenkstätte Deutscher Widerstand upstairs covers the whole German resistance, from church groups to students and workers.
new.tip: Admission is free. Begin in the quiet courtyard with its bronze figure, then go upstairs to the exhibition in the former army offices.

new.title: Sit on Zionskirchplatz, where Bonhoeffer taught
new.desc: August Orth's neo-Romanesque church opened in 1873 on a small hill between Mitte and Prenzlauer Berg. Dietrich Bonhoeffer taught a confirmation class here in 1931, and in 1987 a Stasi raid on the dissident environmental library in its cellar sparked vigils that drew attention across Germany.
new.tip: On Sundays from noon you can usually climb to the tower platform. The leafy square around the church has some of the best-loved café terraces in the neighbourhood.

new.title: Light a thought for 1989 at the Gethsemanekirche
new.desc: In October 1989 this red brick church stayed open day and night under the motto Watch and pray, and thousands gathered with candles outside. The police and Stasi arrested hundreds here on 7 October, weeks before the Wall fell.
new.tip: Look for Ernst Barlach's Geistkämpfer on the south side. The surrounding Gethsemanekiez is one of Prenzlauer Berg's prettiest corners for a slow walk.

new.title: Find Max Liebermann's grave on Schönhauser Allee
new.desc: Opened in 1827, this Jewish cemetery holds about 22,800 graves under tall trees, with the painter Max Liebermann and the composer Giacomo Meyerbeer among those buried here. Along its back wall runs the Judengang, a walled lane whose origins are still debated.
new.tip: Men should cover their heads; the cemetery is closed on Saturdays and Jewish holidays. Enter from Schönhauser Allee, close to U-Bahn Senefelderplatz.
new.q: Jüdischer Friedhof Schönhauser Allee, Schönhauser Allee 23, Berlin

new.title: Trace the star-shaped prison in the Moabit history park
new.desc: A Prussian model prison once stood here, laid out as a star so guards could see every wing from the centre. Albrecht Haushofer wrote his Moabit Sonnets in a cell here in the winter of 1944. Since 2006 the site is a park with a rebuilt cell, old walls and the outline of the star in the paths.
new.tip: It is a few minutes from Hauptbahnhof yet often empty. Step into the concrete cell to hear the sound installation of knocking signals.
new.q: Geschichtspark Ehemaliges Zellengefängnis Moabit, Invalidenstraße, Berlin

new.title: Spot Bruno Taut's red brick estate by the Schillerpark
new.desc: Built between 1924 and 1930, the Siedlung Schillerpark in Wedding has some of Berlin's earliest flat roofs and dark red brick facades inspired by Amsterdam. Since 2008 it has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Berlin's modernist estates.
new.tip: Walk along Bristolstraße and Dubliner Straße to see the loggias, then cross into the Schillerpark itself for a picnic on its big lawns.

new.title: Share a breakfast tower at Café Anna Blume
new.desc: This café on Kollwitzstraße is also a flower shop, so you eat among fresh blooms and buckets of tulips. Its signature is a tiered breakfast stand for two or more, piled with cheeses, spreads, fruit and pastries, plus cakes from its own patisserie.
new.tip: At weekends book or arrive before ten. The terrace on the corner is perfect for watching Prenzlauer Berg go by.

new.title: Find the hidden door of Cookies Cream
new.desc: This vegetarian restaurant with a Michelin star hides in a back alley off Behrenstraße. You follow the lane to a chandelier hanging over a service door, and inside is a tasting menu built entirely from vegetables.
new.tip: As the restaurant itself says, when you think you are lost, you are right. Book ahead; it opens only in the evenings from Tuesday to Saturday.

new.title: Slurp pho at Monsieur Vuong
new.desc: Dat Vuong started serving Vietnamese street food in the Scheunenviertel in 1999, long before it was everywhere in Berlin. The menu at Alte Schönhauser Straße is short and changes twice a week, with the pho always on it.
new.tip: Check the wall boards for the dishes of the day. Finish with a Vietnamese iced coffee.
new.q: Monsieur Vuong, Alte Schönhauser Straße 46, Berlin

new.title: Taste the coffee that started Berlin's third wave at Bonanza
new.desc: Bonanza began roasting specialty coffee in 2006 and helped set off Berlin's coffee boom from this small bar on Oderberger Straße. Baristas pull light-roasted espresso and filter brews from the company's own beans.
new.tip: There are only a few seats, so take your cup to the benches outside. Combine it with a stroll to the Mauerpark at the end of the street.
new.q: Bonanza Coffee Heroes, Oderberger Straße 35, Berlin

new.title: Queue for an ice cream at Hokey Pokey
new.desc: Since 2011 this ice cream patisserie has drawn long lines on Stargarder Straße with flavours like Sicilian pistachio, Valrhona chocolate and Very Cherry. Everything is made in house, and the queue is part of the local summer ritual.
new.tip: The line moves quickly; decide while you wait. In winter some branches pause, but the Stargarder Straße shop usually stays open.

new.title: Eat borscht and blini at Pasternak
new.desc: Across from the old water tower, Pasternak has served Russian, Ukrainian and Jewish cooking since 1994. Expect borscht, pelmeni, herring under a fur coat and blini with sour cream, in a room that feels like an old Moscow café.
new.tip: Weekend brunch is popular and fills up fast. The terrace looks out at the old water tower.

new.title: Order a steak by the Spree at Grill Royal
new.desc: Grill Royal sits on the river bank at Weidendammer Brücke and is Berlin's classic place for steaks, oysters and seeing who else is dining. Prime cuts from several countries are grilled and served with sides to share.
new.tip: Ask for a table on the riverside terrace in summer. It opens at 5 pm; earlier slots are easier to get.

new.title: Dine in the half-timbered house of Paris-Moskau
new.desc: This little half-timbered house dates from the 1890s and once stood alone in a no man's land near the Wall and the old Lehrter Bahnhof. Since 1987 it has been the restaurant Paris-Moskau, with French, German and Russian influences and around 220 wines.
new.tip: The weekday lunch menu is the affordable way in. It is a short walk from Hauptbahnhof and the government quarter.

new.title: Sip a classic cocktail at Becketts Kopf
new.desc: On Pappelallee in Prenzlauer Berg is one of Berlin's most respected cocktail bars, focused on classic drinks made with craft spirits. The room is dim, quiet and made for conversation.
new.tip: It opens from 8 pm Thursday to Saturday, with walk-ins welcome; on other nights the space hosts a different bar. Let the bartenders steer you through the classics.

new.title: Graze through the market on Kollwitzplatz
new.desc: Twice a week the leafy square in Prenzlauer Berg turns into a market: an organic one on Thursdays and a larger general market along Kollwitzstraße on Saturdays. Stalls sell bread, cheese, fish, flowers and plenty of food to eat on the spot.
new.tip: Saturday morning is liveliest. Pick up something to eat and find a bench by Gustav Seitz's statue of Käthe Kollwitz in the middle of the square.

new.title: Have Baumkuchen at Konditorei Buchwald
new.desc: Gustav Buchwald founded this pastry shop in Cottbus in 1852 and became a royal Prussian court supplier; the family later moved it to Berlin. It still bakes Baumkuchen, the layered tree cake, in a gently old-fashioned café by the Moabit end of the Hansaviertel.
new.tip: Order the Baumkuchen with chocolate or sugar glaze and a pot of coffee. It closes for a summer break in mid July, so check before you go.

new.title: Go underground with the Berliner Unterwelten
new.desc: The Berliner Unterwelten association leads tours into war bunkers, Cold War shelters and the shell of the giant flak tower in Volkspark Humboldthain. Many tours start at Gesundbrunnen station, under Berlin's busy streets.
new.tip: Book online and wear closed, sturdy shoes; it stays cool underground all year. The flak tower tours are for adults only.

new.title: Swim in the Strandbad Plötzensee
new.desc: Berliners have bathed in this lake in Wedding since the 1820s, and the lido opened in 1922. A sandy beach and a long curved wall frame the water, all within the city's inner north.
new.tip: Hot afternoons get crowded; come in the morning or early evening. You can walk on around the lake towards the Volkspark Rehberge afterwards.

new.title: Imagine tomorrow at the free Futurium
new.desc: Opened in 2019 next to the Spree, the Futurium is a free museum about the future, asking how we want to live. Interactive rooms cover people, nature and technology, and the rooftop walkway looks over the Reichstag dome and the TV tower.
new.tip: Do not skip the roof. It is closed on Tuesdays and stays open until 8 pm on Thursdays.

new.title: Beat the laser maze at the Deutsches Spionagemuseum
new.desc: On Leipziger Platz, a few steps from the line of the Wall, this museum gathers more than 500 objects from the world of espionage, including two original Enigma machines and Cold War spy cameras. A laser maze tests how agile you are.
new.tip: Allow two hours. The laser maze is the highlight for children, so expect a short queue at weekends.

new.title: See a play at Brecht's Berliner Ensemble
new.desc: The Threepenny Opera premiered in the Theater am Schiffbauerdamm in 1928, and from 1954 Bertolt Brecht and Helene Weigel's company made it their home. The Berliner Ensemble still plays here, with a bronze Brecht sitting on the square outside.
new.tip: Cheap last minute and standing tickets are often available. Even without a show, the plush neo-Baroque foyer is worth a peek.

new.title: Watch a grand revue at the Friedrichstadt-Palast
new.desc: Opened in 1984, the Friedrichstadt-Palast stages lavish revues with over a hundred performers, one of the largest stages in the world and a famously long kickline. Shows mix dance, acrobatics and costume spectacle.
new.tip: Seats in the middle of the stalls give the best view of the stage lifts and water effects. Shows are largely wordless, so language is no barrier.

new.title: Laugh along with 'Gutes Wedding, schlechtes Wedding'
new.desc: The Prime Time Theater in Wedding has been staging its own sitcom, a parody of a TV soap set in the neighbourhood, for two decades, with well over a hundred episodes so far. Locals come back for each new episode like it is a TV series.
new.tip: Shows are in German with heavy Berlin dialect, so it helps to know some. Arrive early for a drink in the bar.

new.title: Catch a concert in the old crematorium at silent green
new.desc: Berlin's first crematorium opened in Wedding in 1912 and closed in 2001. Since 2015 it has been the silent green Kulturquartier, with concerts, films and readings under the dome of the old funeral hall and exhibitions in a vast underground concrete hall.
new.tip: Check the programme before you go. Even on a quiet day the courtyard and the café-restaurant Mars are worth a visit.

new.title: Visit the villa of the Wannsee Conference
new.desc: In this lakeside villa on 20 January 1942, senior Nazi officials met to coordinate the murder of Europe's Jews. Since 1992 the Haus der Wannsee-Konferenz has been a memorial and education centre, with the original conference room at its heart.
new.tip: Admission is free. Allow time to read the protocol on display, then step into the garden for a quiet moment by the water.
new.q: Haus der Wannsee-Konferenz, Am Großen Wannsee 56-58, Berlin

new.title: Walk into Max Liebermann's painted garden
new.desc: Max Liebermann spent his summers from 1910 in this villa on the Wannsee and painted its flower garden about 200 times. Since 2006 it has been a museum with around 40 of those paintings in his upstairs studio, and the garden has been replanted to match them.
new.tip: Come between June and September when the hedge gardens and the birch path are at their best. The terrace café looks across the lawn to the lake.

new.title: See Berlin's oldest palace at Jagdschloss Grunewald
new.desc: Elector Joachim II laid the foundation stone of this white hunting lodge on the Grunewaldsee in 1542, making it the oldest surviving palace in Berlin. Inside hangs the city's largest collection of works by Lucas Cranach and his workshop.
new.tip: Pair the visit with a walk around the Grunewaldsee, one of the city's favourite places to walk dogs. The palace is mostly open in the warmer months.

new.title: See expressionist colour at the Brücke-Museum
new.desc: Opened in 1967 in a low pavilion at the edge of the Grunewald, the Brücke-Museum holds the world's largest collection of the Brücke group, founded in Dresden in 1905. Karl Schmidt-Rottluff's own donation started the collection.
new.tip: It is small, so you can see it all in an hour. Walk a few minutes to the Kunsthaus Dahlem next door, then on into the forest.

new.title: Visit sculptor Georg Kolbe's studio in Westend
new.desc: Georg Kolbe had this brick studio built in 1928 and 1929, two cubes around a sculpture garden among pine trees. It has been a museum since 1950, showing his work and changing exhibitions of modern sculpture.
new.tip: The café Benjamine in the neighbouring house is a lovely stop. Combine the visit with the Olympiastadion, a short walk away.
new.q: Georg Kolbe Museum, Sensburger Allee 25, Berlin

new.title: Stand at the Gleis 17 memorial in Grunewald
new.desc: From Grunewald station, trains deported Berlin's Jews to the ghettos and death camps from October 1941. Since 1998 the old platform of track 17 has been lined with cast iron plates giving the date, number of people and destination of every transport.
new.tip: Walk the whole length of the platform; the track itself is left overgrown, a sign that no train will leave from here again. It is reached through the station underpass, follow the signs.

new.title: Find the Brothers Grimm in Schöneberg's old cemetery
new.desc: The Alter St.-Matthäus-Kirchhof opened in 1856 and is the resting place of Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, the doctor Rudolf Virchow and the singer Rio Reiser. At the entrance, Café Finovo was Germany's first cemetery café.
new.tip: The Grimm graves are side by side near the middle of the cemetery. Have a coffee and cake at Café Finovo by the gate afterwards.

new.title: Leave a flower for Marlene Dietrich in Friedenau
new.desc: Marlene Dietrich, born in Schöneberg, was buried in this small cemetery on Stubenrauchstraße in 1992, close to her mother. Helmut Newton lies nearby, and the composer Ferruccio Busoni's grave carries a bronze figure by Georg Kolbe.
new.tip: Her grave is usually decorated with fresh flowers. Ask at the entrance or look for the honorary grave signs.

new.title: Wander the colourful estate of Onkel Toms Hütte
new.desc: On the edge of the Grunewald, Bruno Taut, Hugo Häring and Otto Rudolf Salvisberg built this garden estate between 1926 and the early 1930s. Its bright colours earned it the nickname parrot estate, and the U-Bahn station has a 1930s shopping arcade built into it.
new.tip: Walk from the station down Argentinische Allee and into the side streets of row houses. The forest and the Krumme Lanke lake are a few minutes away.

new.title: Explore Spandau's old town around St. Nikolai
new.desc: The Gothic hall church of St. Nikolai has stood at the heart of Spandau's old town since the 14th century. Here on 1 November 1539, Elector Joachim II took Protestant communion, bringing the Reformation to Brandenburg.
new.tip: Wander the lanes of the old town afterwards, especially the Kolk quarter by the Havel. In Advent the streets around the church fill with one of Berlin's biggest Christmas markets.

new.title: Dine among the artworks at the Paris Bar
new.desc: Opened in 1950 by a former cook of the French forces, the Paris Bar on Kantstraße became the meeting place of West Berlin's artists. Under Michel Würthle the walls filled with art, and in 2005 the sale of a Kippenberger painting saved the place.
new.tip: Order the French bistro classics and look at the art crowding every wall. Book for the evening, or slip in for a drink at the bar.

new.title: Eat Berlin home cooking at the Dicke Wirtin
new.desc: Just off Savignyplatz, this old Berlin pub is named after Anna Stanscheck, the generous landlady who fed art students with her stews. It still serves Eisbein with sauerkraut, meatballs with fried potatoes and Schmalz on bread.
new.tip: The weekday lunch is great value. It is closed on Tuesdays.

new.title: Book a special dinner at Bieberbau
new.desc: Hidden in a residential street in Wilmersdorf, Bieberbau serves creative fine dining in a listed building from 1894, with richly decorated stucco walls. Chef Stephan Garkisch and Anne Garkisch run it with wine pairings and warm service.
new.tip: It opens only in the evenings, so reserve. Take a moment to look at the stucco: it is one of the most beautiful dining rooms in the city.

new.title: Taste Pfalz wines at the Kurpfalz Weinstuben
new.desc: A Charlottenburg institution since 1935, this wine tavern pours more than 50 wines by the glass and keeps a cellar of around 800 bottles, mostly German and especially from the Pfalz. The food is hearty regional cooking.
new.tip: Ask for an older vintage by the glass. It opens from 4 pm, Tuesday to Saturday.

new.title: Grab an organic Currywurst at Witty's
new.desc: Across from the KaDeWe on Wittenbergplatz, Witty's sells Currywurst made from organic meat, with crisp fries and its own sauces. It is a quick, honest stop between department store and U-Bahn.
new.tip: It stays open until midnight most nights. Try the sausage without skin, the old West Berlin way.

new.title: Drink a Havelbräu at the Brauhaus Spandau
new.desc: For over 30 years this brewpub near Spandau's old town has brewed its Havelbräu in copper kettles, with seasonal beers alongside. The beer garden sits right next to the brewery.
new.tip: Combine it with the Zitadelle or the old town. Hearty Berlin and Bavarian dishes go well with the house beer.

new.title: Have a beer by the water at the Fischerhütte am Schlachtensee
new.desc: A fisherman's hut stood on the shore of the Schlachtensee in the 18th century, and the inn that grew from it is now a listed building. Its lakeside beer garden opens daily and serves beer with Weißwurst and pretzels.
new.tip: Walk the lake loop first, then reward yourself here. On sunny weekends come before noon to find a table by the water.

new.title: Watch the boats at the Schleusenkrug
new.desc: Tucked by the lock of the Landwehrkanal on the western edge of the Tiergarten, the Schleusenkrug is a beer garden and café with views of the boats passing through. It is just a few minutes on foot from Zoo station, yet feels like the countryside.
new.tip: In winter it keeps shorter daytime hours, with indoor seats facing the lock. In summer, grab a table at the water's edge.

new.title: Lunch with a book at the Joseph-Roth-Diele
new.desc: This cosy café-restaurant on Potsdamer Straße is named after the Austrian writer Joseph Roth, who chronicled Berlin in the 1920s. Locals come for its good-value weekday lunch in a relaxed, bookish room.
new.tip: It is open Tuesday to Friday only. Arrive before one to get a table at lunchtime.

new.title: Take the little ferry to the Pfaueninsel
new.desc: King Friedrich Wilhelm II built a white fairy-tale palace here in the 1790s for his companion Wilhelmine Encke. Today peacocks roam free across the car-free island in the Havel, part of the UNESCO site with Potsdam's palaces.
new.tip: The ferry runs about every 15 minutes. Dogs, bikes and picnicking off the paths are not allowed, so bring a snack and stick to the trails.

new.title: Rent a beach chair at the Strandbad Wannsee
new.desc: Opened in 1907, the Strandbad Wannsee has more than a kilometre of sandy beach, wicker beach chairs to rent and listed terraced buildings from 1929 and 1930. It is one of Europe's largest inland lidos.
new.tip: Hire a Strandkorb for the day if the sun is strong. On summer weekends take the S-Bahn to Nikolassee and walk through the forest.

new.title: Cross the Wannsee on the F10 ferry to Kladow
new.desc: The BVG ferry F10 crosses the Großer Wannsee to the village of Kladow in about 20 minutes, sailing every hour all year. It costs nothing more than a normal Berlin AB ticket.
new.tip: Buy your ticket at the machine at Wannsee harbour before boarding. In Kladow, walk along the shore and have a drink before taking the ferry back.

new.title: Walk or swim around the Schlachtensee
new.desc: This long forest lake has a 5.5 km shore path that is one of Berlin's favourite jogging and walking routes. Its clear water and wooded banks make it a popular place to swim in summer.
new.tip: Start at S-Bahnhof Schlachtensee. On hot days the small beaches on the south side are calmer than those by the station.

new.title: Step into the tropics at the Botanischer Garten
new.desc: Covering more than 43 hectares with about 22,000 plant species, Berlin's Botanischer Garten is one of the largest in the world. Its Great Tropical House from 1907 is about 25 metres high.
new.tip: Head straight for the Great Tropical House on a grey day. Use the Unter den Eichen entrance if coming by bus, or Königin-Luise-Platz from the S-Bahn side.

new.title: Visit the farm with its own U-Bahn stop at Domäne Dahlem
new.desc: Domäne Dahlem is an organic farm and open-air museum around a manor house from 1560, one of the oldest in Berlin. It is said to be Germany's only farm with a U-Bahn connection, at Dahlem-Dorf.
new.tip: Children love the animals and the fields. The harvest festival in autumn and the Advent markets draw crowds from across the city.

new.title: Catch a summer concert in the Waldbühne
new.desc: Built for the 1936 Olympics, the Waldbühne is an open-air amphitheatre for about 22,000 people set in a wooded hollow. The Berlin Philharmonic's annual concert here is a summer highlight, ending with the crowd whistling along to Berliner Luft.
new.tip: Bring a cushion and a picnic. Tickets for the Philharmonic concert sell out months ahead.

new.title: Watch the monkeys from the Bikini Berlin terrace
new.desc: The Bikini-Haus from the 1950s got its nickname from an open middle floor that split it in two. Reopened in 2014 as a concept mall, it has a public terrace on the north side that looks straight into the zoo's monkey enclosure.
new.tip: The terrace is free and open during mall hours. Bring a takeaway from the food hall downstairs.

new.title: Climb the Grunewaldturm for a view over the Havel
new.desc: Built between 1897 and 1899 to honour Kaiser Wilhelm I, this brick tower by Franz Schwechten stands high above the Havel. About 204 steps lead to a viewing platform 36 metres up with wide views over the river and forest.
new.tip: Come late in the afternoon for the light on the water. The Havelchaussee bus stops right by the tower.
